title: GDP, (Second Estimate) and Corporate Profits, 3rd Quarter 2026
body: News Release Explore Product View News Release Related Materials Contacts EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EST, Wednesday, November 25, 2026 BEA 26–50 GDP (Second Estimate) and Corporate Profits, 3rd Quarter 2026 Real gross domestic product  (GDP ) increased  at an annual rate of 4.3 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July,  August, and September), according to the second estimate released today by the  U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased  2.2 percent. The contributors to the increase  in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in  investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset  by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation  of GDP, increased. Real GDP was  revised up 0.9 percentage point from the advance estimate, primarily reflecting  upward revisions to investment and consumer spending. For more information,  refer to the " Technical Notes " below. Compared to the second  quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily  reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending  that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the  third quarter than in the second quarter. Real final sales to private  domestic purchasers , the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment,  increased 5.8 percent in the third quarter, revised up 0.9  percentage point from the previous estimate. The price index for gross domestic  purchases increased  2.7 percent in the third quarter, revised down 0.3 percentage point  from the previous estimate. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE)  price index increased 2.1 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding  food and energy increased 2.5 percent, both the same as previously  estimated. Real gross domestic income  (GDI) increased 4.4 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase  of 2.3 percent (revised) in the second quarter. The average of real GDP and  real GDI also increased 4.4 percent, compared with an increase of 2.2  percent (revised). Profits from current  production (corporate profits with inventory valuation and capital consumption  adjustments) increased $206.0 billion in the third quarter, compared  with an increase of $384.0 billion in the second quarter. Real GDP and Related Measures [Percent  change (SAAR) from 2026:Q2 to 2026:Q3] Advance Estimate Second Estimate Real GDP 3.4 4.3 Current-dollar GDP 5.6 6.2 Real final sales to private domestic purchasers 4.9 5.8 Real GDI … 4.4 Average of real GDP and real GDI … 4.4 Gross domestic purchases price index 3.0 2.7 PCE price index 2.1 2.1 PCE price index excluding food and energy 2.5 2.5 SAAR seasonally adjusted at annual rates U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis For definitions, statistical conventions, updates to GDP, and more information about national statistics, visit " Additional Information ." Next release: December 23, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. EST GDP (Third Estimate), Industries, Corporate Profits, State GDP, and  State Personal Income, 3rd Quarter 2026 The full release  schedule for 2027 is available on BEA's website . As part of ongoing  efforts to modernize and streamline news release packages, BEA will no longer  produce identical versions of this news release in both PDF and HTML formats.  Starting in January 2027, this news release will be posted to the website in HTML  only. Technical Notes Sources of revision to real GDP Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 4.3 percent (1.1 percent at a quarterly rate 1 )  in the third quarter, an upward revision of 0.9 percentage point  from the previous estimate, primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment  and consumer spending. The revision to investment was led by an upward  revision to intellectual property products, notably software, based primarily  on revisions to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Producer Price Index for  system and application software publishing, excluding maintenance, tech support  and games. The revision to consumer spending reflected an  upward revision to goods that was partly offset by a downward revision to  services. Within goods, the upward revision was led by  other nondurable goods (mainly pharmaceuticals), recreational goods and  vehicles (mainly computer software and accessories), and gasoline and other  energy goods, based on revised data from the U.S. Census Bureau Monthly Retail  Trade Survey and new and revised data from the U.S. Department of Energy. Within services, the largest contributor to the  downward revision was health care (both hospital and nursing home services and outpatient  services), based on newly available third-quarter U.S. Census Bureau Quarterly  Services Survey data. More  information on the source data and BEA assumptions that underlie the third-quarter  estimate is shown in the key  source data and assumptions table. Related Data Tables For the estimates highlighted in this release, as well as historical  time series for these estimates, see the following data tables in BEA’s Interactive Data Application . title: Bowman, Modernizing Banking Supervision: A Shared Agenda for the Americas
body:
﻿ Speech by Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman on modernizing banking supervision: a shared agenda for the Americas - Federal Reserve Board Skip to main content An official website of the United States Government Here's how you know Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 25, 2026 Modernizing Banking Supervision: A Shared Agenda for the Americas Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman At the ASBA–BCBS–FSI High-Level Meeting for the Americas on Banking Supervision, Brasília, Brazil (via pre-recorded video) Share Accessible Keys for Video [Space Bar] toggles play/pause; [Right/Left Arrows] seeks the video forwards and back (5 sec ); [Up/Down Arrows] increase/decrease volume; [M] toggles mute on/off; [F] toggles fullscreen on/off (Except IE 11); The [Tab] key may be used in combination with the [Enter/Return] key to navigate and activate control buttons, such as caption on/off. Good morning. 1 I would like to thank our hosts, the Banco Central do Brasil, the Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas (ASBA), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), and the Financial Stability Institute, for bringing us together. Banking supervisors around the world are tasked with ensuring the safety and soundness of the banking system. To be effective in this work, bank supervisory and regulatory frameworks must be forward looking to anticipate future risks. Today, I will discuss three ways in which modernizing our supervision and regulatory frameworks can enhance our ability to be effective. First, we must learn the appropriate lessons from failures of supervisory effectiveness. Recent experience in the United States demonstrates that it is not sufficient to identify financial risks. Supervisors must also have the authority, accountability, and judgment to act before those risks are realized. Second, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must be regularly revisited to keep pace with the evolving financial landscape. These frameworks must focus on the most material risks, enable timely decisions, and adapt to rapidly changing financial markets and technologies. This is a priority both for the Federal Reserve and our international colleagues, including those on the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the BCBS. Third, banking supervisors throughout the Americas must be effective. Our shared history, deeply interconnected economies, and regional financial challenges support alignment of our interests in maintaining strong institutions for supervisory cooperation. ASBA can play a role in that effort. These points are closely related. Effective supervision requires sound judgment. Sound judgment must be supported by modern frameworks. And cooperation among supervisors in the Americas supports strengthening both. Learning from Banking Failures: Information Must Lead to Action One of the most valuable responsibilities of any supervisory authority is to learn the right lessons from failure and adjust accordingly. The March 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), and subsequent discussions about what went wrong and paths for reform, provide a useful case study. Extraordinary measures were taken to address banking system stress in the wake of SVB's failure, and fundamental questions remain regarding the effectiveness of the Federal Reserve System's supervisory function. Earlier reviews of the bank's failure provided important information but did not consider questions about shortcomings in the Federal Reserve's supervisory approach or identify opportunities to address long-standing weaknesses in our supervision. When I became Vice Chair for Supervision, I initiated an independent review of SVB's failure. The initial findings of that review released in September were sobering. The review validated that supervisors identified the bank's fundamental vulnerabilities well before its failure. 2 Those vulnerabilities included substantial interest rate risk, a highly concentrated and predominantly uninsured deposit base, and inadequate preparedness to meet liquidity demands. These were not unfamiliar or complicated risks to understand. They have been common risks throughout history, were present at the time of SVB's failure, and continue to be fundamental banking risks today. Yet our supervisory process failed to produce timely and effective action to address them. A central lesson is that the failure of supervision was not a failure to obtain information. It was a failure to translate information into timely, decisive action. The review identified a long-standing supervisory problem of consultation without conclusion or action, uncertainty about decisionmaking authority, and a lack of accountability. Supervisors identified concerns, documented weaknesses, and discussed vulnerabilities. But the process did not result in prompt action to require the bank to address material risks that ultimately led to its failure. One particularly revealing finding illustrates the problem. Between 2019 and March 2023, supervisors cited 54 supervisory matters that required attention. Yet no finding required SVB to shorten the maturity profile of its securities portfolio or restructure the held-to-maturity book, which were material financial risks that contributed to the bank's failure. Instead, many supervisory findings focused on process concerns. While interest rate risk was discussed, the approach criticized how the bank measured the risk but did not direct the bank to reduce it. Supervisors engaged in extensive supervisory activity, produced considerable documentation, and created a substantial record of identified concerns. But the risks that were most material—the risks that affected the bank's financial condition—were not addressed. This experience should encourage every supervisory authority to consider how it measures its own effectiveness. We should not measure success by the number of examinations conducted, findings issued, and reports produced. Instead, we must measure success by whether our work results in the timely identification, mitigation, and remediation of material risks. A supervisory organization can be extraordinarily busy without being effective. Excessive process can become a major obstacle to effective supervision. When responsibility is unclear, when decisionmaking authority is fragmented, or when supervisors believe that every judgment must be supported by perfect information, the supervisory process can delay action until it is too late. The independent review showed that these organizational and cultural weaknesses can have serious consequences. Supervisory decisions must be grounded in sound analysis, appropriate legal authority, and professional judgment. But those decisions must also be timely. A supervisory judgment that arrives after the opportunity for effective intervention has passed may have little practical value. Our goal must be to reach reasonably informed decisions in time to influence outcomes, rather than achieving perfect certainty after the opportunity to act has passed. This lesson becomes even more important as supervisory authorities adopt new technology. Artificial intelligence (or super intelligence), advanced analytics, and other supervisory technologies have the potential to improve the identification of emerging risks and our understanding of complex financial relationships. This can provide supervisors access to more information more quickly than ever before. But more information is not necessarily better supervision. The SVB experience should remind us that information alone is not a substitute for judgment and timely action. Therefore, our approach must be to modernize supervisory culture while upgrading our supervisory technology. Clear lines of responsibility and decisionmaking authority are imperative. The ultimate measure of successful and effective supervision is the ability to recognize material risks and act effectively while there is still time to influence the outcome. Modernizing Our Supervisory and Regulatory Frameworks Second, we must ensure our regulatory and supervisory frameworks enable the identification of material risks, sound decisionmaking, and supervisory response in a rapidly changing financial system. Our priorities should be to ensure supervisors are trained to identify and focus attention on material risks, enable timely decisionmaking and clear accountability, and establish a regulatory framework that encourages innovation without compromising safety and soundness. The Federal Reserve is pursuing each of these objectives. First, we are modernizing the conduct of supervision. Our Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles refocuses supervision on identifying material risks and taking prompt, proportionate action to address them. The principles emphasize risk-focused supervision, tailored to the size, complexity, and risk profile of individual institutions. They call for clearer expectations, greater transparency, and the exercise of sound professional judgment rather than excessive reliance on procedural requirements, checklists, or documentation. They also seek to align examination findings and supervisory ratings more closely with material risks, reduce unnecessary duplication, and streamline the resolution of supervisory concerns. Our objective is not to produce more supervisory findings or more documentation. It is to ensure that supervision identifies the risks that matter most and results in timely action to address them. 3 Second, we are changing how we organize the supervisory function itself. The independent review highlighted a fundamental organizational weakness, a mismatch between decisionmaking authority and accountability. The Federal Reserve's supervisory responsibilities have historically been carried out through a complex structure involving the Board, the 12 Reserve Banks, and numerous committees. That structure has not always provided accountability, identified clear lines of responsibility, or supported timely decisions. To address these shortcomings, we have begun reorganizing our supervisory function. The reorganization preserves the expertise and relationships of local examination teams while providing clearer lines of accountability through regional leadership. This reorganization is intended to clarify decisionmaking authority, streamline escalation, reduce unnecessary layers of review, and strengthen accountability for supervisory outcomes. We are also examining the role of committees and other internal processes that can cloud responsibility or delay action. When supervisors identify a material risk, there should be no ambiguity about who has the authority to act, who is responsible for ensuring that action is taken, and the importance of elevating decisions for prompt action when necessary. 4 Third, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must keep pace with innovation. Financial markets and technology are evolving rapidly. Artificial intelligence, digital assets, payment technology, and innovative business models create opportunities to improve efficiency, expand financial services, and support economic growth. Our responsibility is to establish clear and predictable rules of the road so that financial institutions can confidently pursue responsible innovation while managing the material risks associated with new activities. This requires a careful balance. Regulatory frameworks that are overly prescriptive or unnecessarily burdensome can discourage innovation, limit competition, and push financial activity outside the regulated banking system. But uncertainty about regulatory expectations can also discourage innovation. Financial institutions need to understand the standards that apply to new activities and the risks they are expected to manage. A modern regulatory framework should provide clarity about objectives and expectations while allowing sufficient flexibility for financial institutions to develop new products, adopt new technology, and respond to changing market conditions. These three elements—risk-focused supervision, clear organizational accountability, and adaptable regulation—are also central to the broader international modernization agenda. As chair of the FSB's Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation, I have worked with colleagues from around the world to develop common principles to guide modernization efforts. In October, the FSB released a consultation report proposing eight high-level principles intended to help authorities improve the effectiveness, efficiency, risk focus, coherence, and adaptability of their regulatory and supervisory frameworks. The principles recognize that our frameworks must remain responsive to emerging financial risks and technological developments. They emphasize appropriate tailoring, transparency, and accountability as well as the importance of periodically evaluating whether regulatory requirements remain fit for their intended purposes. As the FSB and the BCBS carry this work forward, they must take care that the assumptions underlying work commissioned in response to bank failures like that of SVB are appropriately validated. Post-failure analyses can embed untested assumptions about what went wrong and what should be done about it, and those assumptions can then be relied upon to shape international standards. Before such conclusions inform global policy, they should be tested against the evidence and confirmed across different jurisdictions and banking models. Importantly, the principles acknowledge that implementation must reflect national legal frameworks and circumstances. 5 That recognition is especially relevant to the Americas, where banking systems differ considerably in their size, structure, complexity, and economic roles. Modernization does not require every jurisdiction to adopt identical institutional arrangements or supervisory practices. It should provide a common set of principles that can be implemented effectively within different financial systems. What matters is that our frameworks produce the outcomes we need: timely identification and mitigation of material risks, clear accountability, predictable regulatory expectations, and the flexibility to respond to change. Strengthening the Supervisory Community in the Americas The third and final topic for my discussion today is the importance of strengthening practical cooperation among the community of supervisors in the Americas. This priority has taken on particular importance in light of recent developments in banking systems throughout the hemisphere. Recent episodes of banking stress serve as a reminder of how quickly financial vulnerabilities can become more serious, and how important the strength and credibility of supervisory institutions can be to maintaining public confidence. They also underscore the broader lesson that effective supervision depends not simply on the existence of rules, but on the ability of institutions and their supervisors to implement those rules, exercise sound judgment, and take action when it is needed. They also provide further support for strengthening the relationships, technical capabilities, and practical cooperation among supervisors across our hemisphere. But there is another reason why cooperation among the countries of the Americas deserves particular attention. The Americas are a community of countries with deep historical, commercial, financial, and institutional connections. Our banking systems are linked through trade finance, investment, cross-border lending, payments, and remittances. Economic developments in one part of the hemisphere can have direct and sometimes immediate consequences for financial institutions and communities elsewhere in the region. These connections support economic growth and financial development. But they also create transmission channels for financial stability risks. We have seen this repeatedly throughout our shared history. The Latin American debt crisis of the 1980s provides one important example. 6 As debt-servicing difficulties spread across Latin America, they posed serious challenges both for the countries directly affected and for international banks with significant exposures throughout the region. The response required extensive cooperation among governments, central banks, commercial banks, and international financial institutions. That cooperation was indispensable. However, the crisis imposed enormous economic costs, and some responses delayed the resolution of underlying vulnerabilities. The experience demonstrated a fundamental reality—that financial stability risks do not respect national boundaries, and effective responses often require close cooperation among authorities across borders. More than four decades later, financial relationships throughout the Americas have become more extensive and complex. But our common interests extend beyond managing financial stability. Our banking systems confront a range of shared challenges, including exposure to cross-border capital flows, commodity cycles, exchange rate movements, and shifts in international financing conditions. Our shared challenges also include the opportunities and risks associated with digital banking, new payments technology, and the growing use of artificial intelligence. There are also challenges that have a particularly significant regional dimension, like remittances and cross-border payments that are critically important to households and businesses throughout the Americas. The efficiency, accessibility, and integrity of these financial channels have important implications for financial inclusion and economic opportunity. At the same time, financial institutions and supervisors must contend with threats arising from money laundering, fraud, illicit financial networks, and transnational criminal organizations. These threats can permeate borders, crossing multiple jurisdictions, and place significant demands on supervisory resources. These threats reinforce the importance of strong supervisory relationships, effective information sharing, and coordination among authorities. International standard-setting bodies such as the Basel Committee, the FSB, and the Financial Stability Institute offer useful reference points and forums for dialogue. Global standards can be a helpful input. But they do not replace the working relationships, regional knowledge, and practical coordination that develop among authorities facing common challenges. They work best when they acknowledge and incorporate national and regional circumstances. This is where I see a valuable role for ASBA. It can provide a forum devoted to the financial systems, supervisory challenges, and institutional relationships of the Americas. Its strength is its regional focus. Bringing together supervisors from across the hemisphere, ASBA can help ensure that our regional priorities receive the attention they deserve, that our supervisory authorities develop the capabilities they need, and that the practical experience of each member country informs the continuing development of international supervisory standards. We should continue building on this important role for ASBA. I see several opportunities to strengthen that role. First, we should deepen the exchange of practical supervisory lessons. The experience of SVB demonstrates why this is important. We should be willing to carefully examine bank failures and supervisory challenges, identify the institutional and operational factors that contributed to them, and determine how those lessons can improve supervisory practice. These exchanges should go beyond identifying vulnerabilities in individual institutions. They should examine how supervisors make decisions, how concerns are escalated, and how institutional arrangements can either facilitate or delay effective action. ASBA can facilitate that exchange through case studies, technical discussions, and practical training. Second, we should strengthen supervisory leadership and institutional capabilities. Technical expertise is essential to effective bank supervision. But the ability to identify risks is only part of the job. Supervisors must also be able to prioritize competing concerns, exercise professional judgment, communicate difficult conclusions, and take timely action. These capabilities can be strengthened through leadership development, secondments, professional exchanges, and realistic supervisory exercises. Strong supervisory institutions also require clear governance arrangements, well-defined responsibilities, and accountability for decisions. Building these capabilities should be an important focus of our regional cooperation. Third, we should cooperate more closely on emerging technologies and new financial activities. Artificial intelligence, digital banking, cybersecurity, and innovative payments technologies present many of the same questions for supervisors throughout the hemisphere. How can these technologies improve risk identification and supervisory efficiency? How should supervisors evaluate the risks associated with new business models? These questions will benefit from practical cooperation. There is significant value in sharing experience with supervisory technologies, analytical methods, and approaches to emerging risks, rather than requiring every authority to develop solutions independently. Fourth, we should continue strengthening cross-border crisis preparedness and supervisory relationships. Relationships established during stable periods can become indispensable as financial conditions deteriorate. When an internationally active bank encounters serious difficulties, timely communication through previously established channels for cooperation can make a meaningful difference. Supervisors should understand the responsibilities of their counterparts, have established mechanisms for exchanging appropriate information, and be prepared to coordinate when circumstances require it. We should continue investing in those relationships now. Finally, I believe the Americas should play an active role in shaping the international modernization agenda. The FSB's proposed principles create an important opportunity for this engagement. ASBA can help bring practical supervisory experience into international discussions, identify implementation challenges, and contribute to improving the effectiveness of international standards. Regional cooperation should not simply be a mechanism for transmitting standards developed elsewhere. It should also help inform the continuing development and practical implementation of those standards. As we pursue regulatory and supervisory modernization, I hope that ASBA will continue to be an active partner in this work. The Federal Reserve values its relationships with supervisory authorities throughout the Americas, and we look forward to strengthening those relationships through ASBA and our other bilateral and multilateral partnerships. Together, our objective should be to strengthen supervisory effectiveness, improve the resilience of our banking systems, and support the financial intermediation that is essential to economic prosperity. In the Americas, we have a special opportunity to do that together by strengthening our supervisory capabilities, deepening our cooperation, and ensuring that ASBA remains responsive to the distinctive needs and priorities of our region. Closing Thoughts The lessons of SVB are clear: identifying risk is not enough. Supervision succeeds only when information leads to timely, decisive action. As we modernize our frameworks, we must focus on material risks, establish clear accountability, and remain adaptable to innovation, while recognizing that each jurisdiction will implement these principles in ways suited to its individual system. I will conclude with a call to use venues like ASBA to share the hard lessons of failure, to build supervisory leadership and capability, to cooperate on emerging technology, and to invest now in the cross-border relationships needed in a crisis. Let us bring these shared experiences into the FSB's modernization work, so that the principles reflect the realities of the Americas. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text 2. See Michelle W. title: Sex offender sentenced to 15 years in federal prison for sexual abuse of minors
body: Press Release Sex offender sentenced to 15 years in federal prison for sexual abuse of minors Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Wyoming usawy.pio@usdoj.gov CHEYENNE, Wyo. — Reland Paul Littleshield Sr. , 52, of Arapahoe, Wyoming, has been sentenced to 15 years in federal prison, followed by fifteen years of supervised release, for sexual abuse and attempted aggravated sexual abuse. Chief U.S. District Court Judge Kelly H. Rankin imposed the sentence. According to court documents, the offenses involved separate, predatory incidents of sexual assault and attempted aggravated sexual abuse targeting two minors on the Wind River Indian Reservation. In both cases, Littleshield deliberately supplied the minors with alcohol until they were severely intoxicated or unconscious before transporting them to his residence in Arapahoe. Once at the home, he physically overpowered, restrained, and sexually assaulted the incapacitated victims while they were unable to consent or escape. Littleshield pleaded guilty to two federal Class A felony counts: one count of sexual abuse and one count of attempted aggravated sexual abuse. “Preying on children is a depraved and cowardly act that inflicts lifelong trauma” said U.S. Attorney Darin Smith. “Littleshield used alcohol as a lure to incapacitate and exploit minors. This 15-year sentence ensures he’ll be removed from society for a decade and a half.” The Bureau of Indian Affairs investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kerry J. Jacobson prosecuted the crime. Case No. 26-CR-00064 ### Updated November 25, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Components Criminal - Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section Criminal - Victim Notification Program Defending Childhood Office of Sex Offender Sentencing, Monitoring, Apprehending, Registering, and Tracking - SMART (OJP) USAO - Wyoming Press Release Number: 26-059

title: Sheridan Man Sentenced to Six-and-a-Half Years in Federal Prison for Receiving Child Sexual Abuse Material
body: Press Release Sheridan Man Sentenced to Six-and-a-Half Years in Federal Prison for Receiving Child Sexual Abuse Material Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Oregon PORTLAND, Ore. — A Sheridan man has been sentenced to six-and-a-half years in federal prison for receiving child sexual abuse material (CSAM), U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced today. David Shawn Elliott , 46, of Sheridan, was sentenced to 78 months in federal prison and 10 years of supervised release. He was also ordered to pay a $100 special assessment and restitution to victims in an amount to be determined. “Child sexual abuse material documents the abuse of real children, and those who seek out, collect, and share it help perpetuate that abuse,” said U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford. “This sentence reflects the serious harm caused by these offenses and our commitment to protecting children and holding offenders accountable.” According to court documents, from December 2023 through May 2024, Elliott participated in multiple online groups dedicated to sharing child sexual abuse material. Through these groups, Elliott accessed images and videos depicting the sexual abuse of prepubescent children as young as 4 and repeatedly requested additional material from other users. Following his arrest, Elliott admitted using an online platform for several years to access and view CSAM. A forensic examination of Elliott’s electronic devices revealed that he had saved child sexual abuse material to his phone. This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Mira Chernick of the District of Oregon. ### Updated November 25, 2026 Component USAO - Oregon

title: Woman From Democratic Republic of Congo Appears in Federal Court for Illegal Voting
body: Press Release Woman From Democratic Republic of Congo Appears in Federal Court for Illegal Voting Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nevada RENO – Mlebinge Riziki Ramadhani, from the Democratic Republic of Congo and a lawful permanent resident, made her initial appearance in federal court Tuesday for allegedly illegally voting in the 2022 General Election. According to a criminal information, on or about November 8, 2022, Ramadhani illegally voted in an election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President, Member of the Senate, and Member of the House of Representatives. She was not a United States citizen. “Federal law is clear that only U.S. citizens are eligible to vote in federal elections,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “Our office will continue to uphold those statutory requirements and ensure accountability whenever federal election laws are violated.” Ramadhani is charged with one count of voting by an alien. She faces a statutory maximum penalty of one year in prison, a fine of up to $100,000, or both. Jury trial is scheduled for January 26, 2027, before United States District Judge Miranda M. Du. The FBI and HSI investigated this case, and the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Nevada is prosecuting the case. An information is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ### Updated November 25, 2026 Topic Voting and Elections Component USAO - Nevada

title: Justice Department Awards Federal Grant to Hire Deputies in Bay County
body: Press Release Justice Department Awards Federal Grant to Hire Deputies in Bay County Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Tallahassee, Florida — Through the Office of Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS Office), the Department of Justice today announced it has awarded nearly $150 million under the 2026 COPS Hiring Program (CHP), including $3.125 million to Bay County. CHP is a competitive grant program that provides funding directly to state, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies to pay for the entry-level salaries and fringe benefits of newly hired and rehired full-time sworn officers/deputies to make America safe again. “Under the leadership of President Trump, violent crime has cratered to record lows,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “We were honored to host President Trump at the Department of Justice today to announce, among other actions, $150 million in grants for state and local law enforcement through the COPS Hiring Program. These funds will put more officers on the beat and keep the American people safe.” U.S. Attorney John P. Heekin said: “Thanks to the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department of Justice continues to invest in our state and local law enforcement partners to provide the critical resources they need on the front lines in our fight against crime. Sheriff Ford and the Bay County Sheriff’s Office are invaluable partners with my office, and I am proud to see these federal grant monies flow into my District to support the hiring of more deputies to keep our communities safe.” “We appreciate our continued partnership with the Department of Justice and their commitment to supporting law enforcement agencies across the country,” said Sheriff Tommy Ford. “Partnerships like these are vital to strengthening public safety and serving our communities.” CHP is a flagship program in the COPS Office, which has a long history of promoting police partnerships. Through CHP, this Administration supports our nation’s front-line heroes by providing them with needed resources and expertise to enhance policing strategies and tactics. The express purpose of CHP is crime reduction through effective common-sense policing. The CHP program focuses on advancing administration priorities. Funding was prioritized for agencies that focused on: Violent Crime, Squatting and Encampment Enforcement, Homeland and Border Security, Nuisance Abatement and Quality of Life, School-Based Policing, and Combating Domestic Terrorism. Additional priority consideration was given to agencies that commit to ending deadly sanctuary city polices, agencies that participate in the Homeland Security Task Force, and agencies that are within rural jurisdictions. Of the selected law enforcement agencies, one hundred and fifty-three recipients will use the funding to focus on violent crime, 40 will focus on school-based policing, 36 will seek to address nuisance abatement and quality of life, 17 will focus on other innovations in common sense policing, 16 will focus on homeland security and seven will focus on squatting and encampment enforcement. The demand for CHP funding remains extremely high among law enforcement agencies nationwide. The COPS Office received 551 requests for funding and was able to award 269 agencies, approximately 49%. More information on the 2026 CHP awards can be found here https://cops.usdoj.gov/chp-award . The COPS Office is the component of the U.S. Department of Justice responsible for advancing the practice of community policing and the Administration’s priority of Making America Safe Again by supporting the nation’s state, local, territorial, and Tribal law enforcement agencies through information and grant resources. To date, the COPS Office has been appropriated more than $21 billion to advance community policing including grants awarded to more than 13,000 state, local, and Tribal law enforcement agencies to fund the hiring and redeployment of more than 141,000 officers. The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General.  To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl Contact United States Attorney’s Office Northern District of Florida USAFLN.Press.Office@usdoj.gov X: @USAO_NDFL Updated November 25, 2026 Topic Grants Components Office of the Attorney General USAO - Florida, Northern

title: Stamford Man Charged with Fentanyl Distribution Offenses
body: Press Release Stamford Man Charged with Fentanyl Distribution Offenses Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Connecticut David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, P.J. O’Brien, Special Agent in Charge of the New Haven Division of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and Stamford Police Chief Timothy Shaw today announced that, on November 23, 2026, a federal grand jury in New Haven returned an indictment charging MARCUS MOORE, 48, of Stamford, with fentanyl distribution offenses. Moore appeared today before U.S. Magistrate Judge Robert M. Spector in New Haven, pleaded not guilty to the charges in the indictment, and was ordered detained. As alleged in court documents and statements made in court, between December 2025 and March 2026, law enforcement made multiple controlled purchases of fentanyl pills from Moore. Moore was arrested yesterday.  Court-authorized searches of Moore’s residence and his vehicle at the time of his arrest revealed fentanyl pills and fentanyl powder, cocaine, narcotics paraphernalia, and a firearm. The indictment charges Moore with three counts of possession with intent to distribute, and distribution of, fentanyl, an offense that carries a maximum term of 20 years on each count, and one count of possession with intent to distribute, and distribution of, 40 grams or more of fentanyl, an offense that carries a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of five years and a maximum term of imprisonment of 40 years.  If convicted of the most serious charge, based on Moore’s alleged criminal history that includes a federal conviction in 2019 for distribution of crack cocaine , Moore faces enhanced penalties of a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 10 years and a maximum term of imprisonment of life. U.S. Attorney Sullivan stressed that an indictment is not evidence of guilt.  Charges are only allegations, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. This investigation is being conducted by the FBI Bridgeport Safe Streets Task Force and the Stamford Police Department.  The Task Force is composed of personnel from the FBI, Connecticut State Police, and the Bridgeport, Fairfield, Norwalk, Trumbull, and Westport Police Departments.  The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Daniel Makofsky and Lauren Clark. Updated November 25, 2026 Topics Drug Trafficking Opioids Component USAO - Connecticut

title: Coralville Man Sentenced to Over 17 Years in Federal Prison for Receipt and Possession of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Coralville Man Sentenced to Over 17 Years in Federal Prison for Receipt and Possession of Child Pornography Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Iowa DAVENPORT, Iowa – A Coralville man was sentenced on November 24, 2026, to 210 months in federal prison for receiving and possessing child pornography. According to public court documents and evidence presented at sentencing, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received CyberTips that an account, later determined to be associated with Jereme Parrish Goltz, 54, received, uploaded, and possessed files containing child sexual abuse material. Law enforcement seized electronic devices during a search of Goltz's Coralville residence. A forensic examination of the seized electronic devices showed that Goltz used the devices to receive, view, and possess images and videos containing child sexual abuse material. After completing his term of imprisonment, Goltz will be required to serve an eight-year term of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system. Goltz was also ordered to pay $15,000 in restitution and $4,000 AVAA Assessment. United States Attorney David C. Waterman of the Southern District of Iowa made the announcement. The Coralville Police Department investigated the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . title: Las Vegas Man Appears in Court for Carjacking Resulting in the Death of Another Man
body: Press Release Las Vegas Man Appears in Court for Carjacking Resulting in the Death of Another Man Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nevada LAS VEGAS – A Las Vegas man made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday for allegedly fatally striking a person during a carjacking. According to a criminal complaint and allegations made in the indictment, on November 10, 2026, Treyvon Leonard Taylor allegedly stole a truck from a residential driveway. The vehicle’s owner tried to stop the theft. Taylor did not stop the truck but instead intentionally struck the victim with the truck before fleeing the scene. “An innocent man is dead because someone decided a vehicle was worth more than a human life,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “That kind of cold-blooded brutality has no place on the streets of Las Vegas. If you terrorize our community with deadly violence, there is nowhere you can hide from federal justice. We will dismantle your life, prosecute you to the absolute fullest extent of the law, and fight relentlessly to ensure you never walk free again.” Taylor is charged with one count of carjacking resulting in death. He is in custody. A trial has been scheduled for January 25, 2027, before United States District Judge Cristina D. Silva. If convicted, he faces a statutory penalty of death. The FBI and Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorneys James Gaeta and Joshua Brister are prosecuting the case. A complaint and an indictment merely contain accusations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ### Updated November 25, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Component USAO - Nevada

title: Merced detective receives Honor the Honorable: The Attorney General’s Award for Distinguished Service in Policing
body: Press Release Merced detective receives Honor the Honorable: The Attorney General’s Award for Distinguished Service in Policing Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of California SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Detective Jennifer Dabney of the Merced Police Department has received the Honor the Honorable: The Attorney General’s Award for Distinguished Service in Policing, one of the Department of Justice's highest honors for state and local law enforcement officers. U.S. Attorney Eric Grant attended the ceremony where Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the award recipients. This award represents the Department of Justice’s reaffirmed commitment to uplifting the valor and exceptional contributions to policing of our great nation’s law enforcement personnel. The awards were given on Friday, November 20, 2026. The Attorney General’s Honor the Honorable Award recognizes rank-and-file enforcement officers from state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies for exceptional policing. Recipients are honored for achievements in criminal investigations, field operations, or community involvement. Within each category, awards were given for small, medium and large jurisdictions. “I was honored to recognize the very best of local law enforcement at the Department of Justice today,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “These men and women are playing a critical role in our effort to Make America Safe Again. The Trump Administration will never apologize for backing the blue and supporting local law enforcement.” “Strong partnerships between federal, state, and local law enforcement are essential to keeping our communities safe,” said Eric Grant. “We are proud to see Detective Jennifer Dabney recognized for her outstanding service to the people of Merced and the broader Eastern District of California. Her dedication reflects the professionalism, commitment, and community-focused policing that make a lasting difference in the lives of those we serve.” “On behalf of the City of Merced, congratulations to Detective Jennifer Dabney on this well-deserved national recognition,” said Steven Stanfield, Merced Police Chief. “We are proud and grateful for the dedication and compassion Detective Dabney brings to her work as a detective. This award is a reflection of the difference she makes in the lives of the people she serves. Merced is fortunate to have Detective Dabney, and we’re honored to celebrate this achievement with her.” Detective Jennifer Dabney of the Merced Police Department was recognized for her leadership in re-establishing the Police Activities League (PAL) in Merced. Over the past two years, she has worked with community leaders, local businesses, and residents to secure and renovate a facility for a new PAL gym, organize fundraising efforts that raised thousands of dollars in support of the program, and develop partnerships to provide opportunities for local youth. Through her efforts, the PAL gym opened in July 2025 and now provides young people with a safe and positive environment where they can build discipline, confidence, teamwork, and other lifelong skills. While leading the PAL revitalization effort, Detective Dabney continued her full-time work as a detective handling complex and sensitive investigations, including sexual assaults and crimes against children. Her commitment to both public safety and youth engagement has strengthened relationships between law enforcement and the Merced community while creating new opportunities for young people. Through her dedication and leadership, she has helped build a program designed to keep youth on a positive path and invest in the future of the community. The 2026 award recipients are as follows: Category: Field Operation. Awards in this category include activities that demonstrate exceptional bravery; heroic, quick, innovative, or otherwise exceptional problem-solving; and sustained excellence in achieving law enforcement goals, engaging in direct action to preserve life, or making a significant arrest. Sergeant Ryan Nichols and Corporal Edwin Bounds of the Forth Worth, Texas, Police Department Officer Jeremiah Harvey, Officer Landen Hopkins, Officer Jason Sikoski, Officer Benjamin Urdiales, and Officer Jeremy Wells of the Tampa, Florida, Police Department Deputy Sheriff Gabriel Fontanez of the Polk County, Floria, Sheriff’s Office Officer Dakota Berry of the Goodyear, Arizona, Police Department Officer Gabriel Rodriguez of the San Bernardino, California, Police Department Corporal Jacob Heatherly, Sergeant Matthew Lynch, and Deputy Devin Mason (posthumous) of the Darlington County, South Carolina, Sheriff’s Office Sergeant Donald Smith of the Chafee County, Colorado, Sheriff’s Office Deputy Kristopher Brakebill of the Okanogan County, Washington, Sheriff’s Office Category: Criminal Investigations. Awards in this category exemplify exceptional innovation, impact, and leadership in solving crimes, preventing future offenses, and improving investigative practices. Master Detective Robert Harrop of the Hillsborough County, Florida, Sheriff’s Department Senior Deputy Phillip Golden of the Harford County, Maryland, Sheriff’s Office Senior Corporal David Roach of the Dallas, Texas, Police Department Detective John Basile and Detective Michelle Stabile of the Danbury, Connecticut, Police Department Detective Jeffrey Stadnicki and Detective Travis Parsons Alachua County, Florida, Sheriff’s Office Detective Travis Schoonover of the Perkasie Borough, Pennsylvania, Police Department Sergeant Robert Lindsey of the Decatur, Georgia, Police Department Category: Exemplary Community Involvement. Awards in this category promote making America’s communities safe again by reducing crimes such as illegal immi­gration, human trafficking, gun crime, drug trafficking, and gang violence. Deputy John Gray of the Arapahoe County, Colorado, Sheriff’s Office Officer Julio Flores of the Dallas, Texas, Police Department Officer William Martinez Jr. of the Chicago Police Department Detective Jennifer Dabney of the Merced, California, Police Department Corporal Laura Gonzalez of the White Settlement, Texas, Police Department Officer Jacob Hubbard of the Bradford, New Hampshire, Police Department The awardees were selected from a nationwide pool of nominees for their outstanding achievements and commitment to making American safe again. title: Defendant sentenced to 27 years in federal prison for armed robbery and firearms-related charges
body: Press Release Defendant sentenced to 27 years in federal prison for armed robbery and firearms-related charges Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Georgia SAVANNAH, Georgia: A Savannah man has been sentenced to prison on federal charges for armed robbery and carjacking. The sentence was imposed by U.S. District Court Chief Judge R. Stan Baker and announced by Margaret E. “Meg” Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia. Eric J. Williams , 38, of Savannah, was sentenced to 324 months in prison followed by five years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Bank Robbery, Possession of a Firearm in Furtherance of a Crime of Violence, and two counts of Carjacking. Williams was also ordered to pay restitution in the amount of $8,693. There is no parole in the federal system. As described in court documents and testimony, in October 2025, Williams entered a Bank of America branch located on Victory Drive in Savannah, wearing dark clothing and a mask and demanding cash from bank tellers while brandishing a Ruger Model Security 9, 9 mm pistol. Williams threatened multiple tellers with the firearm as they placed U.S. currency into a bag. After leaving the rear of the bank with a substantial amount of cash, Williams approached a vehicle while brandishing his firearm and forced his way into the vehicle and attempted to flee, but the vehicle would not shift into gear. Williams then made his way to another vehicle, forcing another victim out and attempted to flee again, but was unsuccessful as the vehicle also became disabled. Savannah Police Department officers responding to the armed robbery call located the defendant based on descriptions provided by witnesses and apprehended Williams. A K-9 officer with the Chatham County Police Department conducted a search of a nearby wooded area and located the stolen cash and firearm. “The rapid coordination between the Savannah Police Department, Chatham County Police K-9 officers, and brave witnesses ensured that this defendant was quickly apprehended and held fully accountable.” said U.S. Attorney Heap. “This 27-year sentence reflects our steadfast commitment to working alongside local law enforcement to keep Savannah safe and hold violent offenders accountable.” This case was investigated in the FBI, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Savannah Police Department, Thunderbolt Police Department, and the Chatham County Police Department. “Eric J. Williams will no longer be able to threaten the safety of our residents but will now serve a lengthy prison sentence that reflects the serious and violent nature of his crimes,” said Brian Ozden, Assistant Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta. “This sentence shows the FBI’s commitment to working with our law enforcement partners to protect all of Georgia against violent crimes.” This case was prosecuted for the United States by Assistant U.S. Attorney Makeia R. Jonese. Contact For any questions, please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Office at (912) 652-4422. title: Washington Man Charged with Coercing Oregon Child to Produce Sexually Explicit Images and Videos
body: Press Release Washington Man Charged with Coercing Oregon Child to Produce Sexually Explicit Images and Videos Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Oregon EUGENE, Ore. — A Washington man has been charged by criminal complaint with coercing an Oregon child to produce sexually explicit images and videos and attempting to receive child sexual abuse material. Patrick Christopher Thompson , 26, of Silverdale, Washington, is charged with attempted production of child pornography, coercion and enticement of a minor, and attempted receipt of child pornography. According to court documents, in June 2023, Thompson allegedly contacted an Oregon preteen through a social media platform. Prosecutors allege that Thompson persuaded the child to send sexually explicit images and later threatened to distribute the images online if the child did not send additional photos and videos. Court documents allege that after obtaining nude images from the child, Thompson used threats and intimidation to compel the child to produce additional sexually explicit content. When the child resisted, Thompson allegedly threatened to share the child's images, personal information, and phone number with members of a large online group. The investigation began after the child's mother reported the conduct to the FBI in June 2023. Investigators later traced online accounts and phone numbers allegedly used in the offenses to Thompson. On Nov. 5, 2026, federal agents executed search warrants at Thompson's residence in Silverdale. During an interview with investigators, Thompson allegedly admitted that, although he did not specifically remember communicating with the preteen, he believed it was something he had done. He also acknowledged threatening to leak the child's images to obtain additional sexually explicit material. Court documents further allege that Thompson admitted receiving similar sexually explicit images and videos from numerous other minors. A criminal complaint is only an accusation of a crime, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. This case is being investigated by the FBI, with assistance from the Washington State Patrol. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Briana Thompson. ### Updated November 25, 2026 Component USAO - Oregon

title: Federal Jury Finds Two Men Guilty on All Counts in Drug Trafficking and Firearms Case
body: Press Release Federal Jury Finds Two Men Guilty on All Counts in Drug Trafficking and Firearms Case Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Minnesota MINNEAPOLIS – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that a federal jury found two defendants guilty on all counts in the case United States v. Charles Edward Legon and Donte Lavell Devers (Case No. 22-cr-332). The verdicts were returned on November 25, 2026, after a seven-day trial before U.S. District Judge Joan N. Ericksen. The defendants and their guilty verdicts include: Charles Edward Legon , aka “Black” and “Chuck,” 45, of Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, was found guilty on seven counts, including (1) one count of conspiracy to distribute fentanyl, (2) conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine, (3) one count of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, (4) one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, (5) one count of conspiracy to possess firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, (6) one count of possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and (7) one count of felon in possession of a firearm. Donte Lavell Devers , aka “Hood,” 45, of Minneapolis, was found guilty on seven counts, including (1) one count of conspiracy to distribute fentanyl, (2) one count of conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine, (3) one count of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, (4) one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, (5) one count of conspiracy to possess firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, (6) one count of possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and (7) one count of felon in possession of a firearm. According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, from in or about August 2021 until August 2022, Legon and Devers conspired to distribute 400 grams or more of fentanyl and 50 grams or more of methamphetamine. In August 2022, both defendants additionally possessed 400 grams or more of fentanyl and 50 grams or more of methamphetamine, with the intention to distribute. Photos of recovered drugs During that time, Legon and Devers also possessed firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. On or about August 3, 2022, Legon possessed a .40 caliber, semi-automatic pistol and Devers possessed a 9mm caliber, semi-automatic pistol. Both defendants on that date were convicted of felonies and could not legally possess firearms. Photos of recovered firearms Devers had been selling drugs in Minneapolis for 25 years. During the time of the conspiracy, Devers was the head of a small “crew” that included several people, including Legon . In February 2022, members of the crew were selling drugs in north Minneapolis and would conduct street sales. The members would often carry a “kit,” which was a collection of many types of drugs for sale. Devers gave these members drugs to sell and they would return money to him after selling. Around February 6, 2022, one of the crew members, Lavell Piggie, aka “Trigga,” suspected another member of the theft of his kit, and the suspicion was shown through text messages that included Devers and other evidence. The suspicion eventually led to Piggie shooting one other crew member and an innocent bystander several times. Piggie then fled the scene and went into hiding, but officers were able to identify him as the suspect and a warrant was issued for his arrest. On February 17, 2022, Devers left the country for a short amount of time, and he left one of his cellphones with Piggie. On February 22, 2022, Piggie was spotted at a big box store in Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. He then engaged law enforcement in a high-speed chase and was apprehended after crashing his car and several law enforcement vehicles. Officers arrested him and found Devers’s cellphone in Piggie’s possession. The cellphone was searched and provided further evidence of the drug trafficking conspiracy among Devers , Legon , Piggie, and others. On July 26, 2022, officers conducted a search of trash behind Devers’s duplex in north Minneapolis. Officers recovered packaging that tested positive for fentanyl and empty pill capsules, and the packaging had Devers’s DNA on it. On August 3, 2022, officers executed search warrants at Devers’s residence in north Minneapolis and Legon’s residence in Brooklyn Park, Minnesota. At Devers’s residence, officers recovered several firearms, including a semi-automatic pistol, a scale, and bank cash wrappers totaling $35,000. The semi-automatic pistol had Devers’s DNA on it. At Legon’s residence, officers recovered cellphones, ammunition, a scale, a semi-automatic pistol, nearly 3 kilograms of fentanyl powder, approximately 10,000 fentanyl pills, 236 grams of methamphetamine, and a kilogram of cocaine. Devers and Legon were both arrested. Photos of recovered drugs, including fentanyl and methamphetamine “Today’s guilty verdicts were the result of a massive undertaking by our federal and local law enforcement partners,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen. “My office will continue to prosecute drug traffickers and dangerous individuals to protect public safety.” “These guilty verdicts reflect the patient, professional, and expert work of MPD investigators and our law enforcement partners in bringing to justice those who distribute the deadly poison of fentanyl and other illicit drugs into our communities. Drug trafficking fuels violence, destroys lives, and harms families and neighborhoods. This case demonstrates our shared commitment to holding offenders accountable and protecting Minneapolis from the devastating effects of drug trafficking and the violence associated with it,” said Minneapolis Police Department Interim Chief Bill Peterson. “These convictions end years of harm to our community,” said HSI St. Paul Special Agent in Charge Travis Pickard. “These convicted felons sold fentanyl and illegally possessed firearms, putting our neighborhoods at risk. HSI and our law enforcement partners held them accountable and made our community safer.” This case was the result of an investigation by the ATF, Minneapolis Police Department, Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, Homeland Security Investigations, Minnesota Department of Corrections Investigation Unit, with assistance from other law enforcement partners. Assistant United States Attorneys David P. Steinkamp and Tory R. Sailer are prosecuting the case. Contact usamn.pressoffice@usdoj.gov Updated November 25, 2026 Topics Drug Trafficking Firearms Offenses Components Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) USAO - Minnesota

title: Walton Man Sentenced to 15 Years for Receipt of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Walton Man Sentenced to 15 Years for Receipt of Child Pornography Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.gov Jerry N. Butler III, 21, of Walton, New York was sentenced on November 24, 2026, by United States District Judge Anthony J. Brindisi to 15 years’ imprisonment, followed by 15 years’ supervised release for receiving child pornography.  First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III and Craig L. Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Albany Field Office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), made the announcement. Butler was charged by information in June 2026 with receiving child pornography.  As part of his guilty plea, Butler admitted that in January and February 2025, he used a social media messaging application to receive child sexual abuse material (CSAM) from an out-of-state minor victim.  Butler exchanged approximately 20,000 messages with the victim in which Butler persuaded the victim to create and send to Butler sexually explicit depictions of herself. Butler accomplished this by, at times, implying to the victim that he would distribute and/or “leak” sexually explicit content of her or would otherwise publicly embarrass her if she did not comply with his demands. In addition to those admissions the investigation into Butler revealed that he was involved in a nihilistic violent extremist (NVE) network, whose members seek to corrupt and exploit vulnerable populations, including minors. Butler was the administrator of an online offshoot of the “764” NVE group that operated across multiple social media channels and whose members engaged in extortion of minors, coercive self-harm, harm to animals, and the production and dissemination of CSAM. Those involved with “764” and related NVE networks methodically target vulnerable, underage populations by using social media to encourage the possession, production, and sharing of extreme gore media and child sexual abuse material (CSAM). Members of NVE groups, including 764, seek to desensitize young people to violence and break down societal norms regarding violence. They normalize the possession, production, and sharing of explicit CSAM and gore material to corrupt and groom their victims toward future violence, gain notoriety among other members of the network, and spread fear for the purpose of accelerating chaos under the NVE ideology with an aim toward the disruption of society. First Assistant United States Attorney Sarcone stated: “The defendant’s reprehensible actions have been met with justice. The online exploitation of minors and manipulation of them into harming themselves is one of the most disturbing threats our nation faces today.  Thanks to the diligent work of our investigative partners FBI, NYSP, and HSI, the defendant will no longer be able to engage in this horrific conduct. He will spend the next 15 years behind bars which is exactly where he belongs.  Behind my leadership and guidance this office has become a national leader in prosecuting 764 cases and will continue to pursue them aggressively thereby protecting the children in our community and communities everywhere.” “Although he was hiding behind a keyboard, Mr. Butler’s sadistic behavior was very real and incredibly damaging,” said Craig Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albany Field Office. “This sentence will keep him behind bars in federal prison for several years. Nihilistic Violent Extremist (NVE) networks like 764 pose an unnerving threat to our most vulnerable, but this case should send a clear message that the FBI Is laser-focused on identifying these abhorrent individuals, investigating them, and sending them to prison where they belong. This case was investigated by the FBI with the assistance of the New York State Police, Walton Police Department, Broome County Sheriff’s Office, and the FBI Atlanta and Milwaukee field offices. Assistant United States Attorney Geoffrey J. L. Brown prosecuted the case as part of Project Safe Childhood. Former Assistant United States Attorney, Senior Litigation Counsel and PSC Coordinator Michael Gadarian also prosecuted the case. Project Safe Childhood is a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys' Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . Updated November 25, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - New York, Northern

title: Columbia Man Charged with Illegal Possession of a Machine Gun
body: Press Release Columbia Man Charged with Illegal Possession of a Machine Gun Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Missouri JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. – A federal grand jury in Jefferson City, Mo., has returned an indictment against a Columbia, Mo. man, for illegally possessing a machine gun. Amillion Mortez Hannah, 18, was charged with possessing a Glock-type machine gun conversion device on Nov. 6, 2026. Hannah had originally been charged by complaint, and the affidavit accompanying the complaint alleged that investigation into a reported robbery on Nov. 5, 2026, led officers to conduct surveillance on Hannah the following morning. Officers saw Hannah place a backpack into a vehicle, and when the backpack was searched, they found a Glock handgun, three drum-style magazines, and a machine gun conversion device inside of it. These devices are considered machine guns and are illegal to possess under federal law. If convicted Hannah could face up to 10 years in prison and fines up to $250,000. The allegations in the indictment are accusations, and not evidence of guilt. Evidence supporting the charges must eventually be presented to a federal trial jury, whose duty it is to determine guilt or innocence. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lauren E. Kummerer. It was investigated by the Columbia Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.
