title: Three Members of Paterson-Based “100k” Gang Plead Guilty to Racketeering Conspiracy for Roles in Murder of Woman; Eight Other Gang Members Pled Guilty to Racketeering Conspiracy Connected to Additional Shootings, Robberies, Drug Trafficking and Bank Fraud
body: Press Release Three Members of Paterson-Based “100k” Gang Plead Guilty to Racketeering Conspiracy for Roles in Murder of Woman; Eight Other Gang Members Pled Guilty to Racketeering Conspiracy Connected to Additional Shootings, Robberies, Drug Trafficking and Bank Fraud Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Jersey NEWARK, N.J. – Eleven members of the Paterson-based neighborhood street gang known as “100k” have pled guilty for their roles in a violent racketeering conspiracy, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced today. “Having spent my career prosecuting violent gangs, I know firsthand the devastation they inflict on our communities. These were not random acts, but calculated crimes committed in furtherance of a violent criminal enterprise. These defendants’ acceptance of responsibility in this case will ensure they are held accountable for their crimes, that some measure of justice is given to the victims and their families, and will make clear to anyone on the street that gang affiliation will not shield those who commit serious crimes from facing the consequences of their actions.” - U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer “ATF remains unwavering in our pursuit of perpetrators of gang violence, and will continue to dismantle criminal enterprises, while using all our resources and partnerships to disrupt the shooting cycle,” said Newark Field Division Special Agent in Charge Beau Kolodka. “These arrests demonstrate ATF’s dedication to working with our local, state, and federal partners in significantly impacting violent gang and drug-related activity that endanger the safety of our communities. Actions like this will not be tolerated. Our unified efforts and commitment are essential to identifying, targeting, and investigating violent criminals who lessen the quality of life in our neighborhoods.” “The pleas demonstrate the unwavering commitment of U.S. Postal Inspectors to dismantling criminal enterprises, protecting the integrity of the U.S. Mail and our employees, and safeguarding the communities we serve,” said U.S. Postal Inspector in Charge Christopher Nielsen. “Through strong law enforcement partnerships, we will continue to identify, investigate, and bring to justice those who engage in organized criminal activity.” On November 23, 2026, Jasun Allah, a/k/a “Rackz,” 22, of Paterson (“J. Allah”), Christopher Thomas, a/k/a “CJ,” 28, of Hackensack, and Michael Davis, a/k/a “Baby 3,” 29, of Paterson, pled guilty to Count One of the Superseding Indictment charging them with conspiracy to violate the Racketeer Influenced Corrupt Organizations statute(“RICO conspiracy”) before Judge Brian R. Martinotti in Newark federal court. This charge relates to the shooting and murder of a Paterson woman identified as Victim-2 in the Superseding Indictment. Eight other individuals previously pled guilty before Judge Martinotti in connection with the Superseding Indictment: Jacim Pitts, a/k/a “Jefe,” 24, of Paterson, pled guilty to RICO conspiracy and conspiracy to distribute controlled substances on September 2, 2026; Elijah Byrd, a/k/a “CEO,” 21, of Paterson, pled guilty to RICO conspiracy on July 1, 2026; Jazmeir Reyes, a/k/a “Baby Joe,” 21, of Paterson, pled guilty to RICO conspiracy, assaulting or impeding a United States employee, and brandishing a weapon in relation to a crime of violence on April 29, 2026; Trasean Short, a/k/a “Hound,” 21, of Elmwood Park, pled guilty to RICO conspiracy on April 28, 2026; Quincy Franklin, a/k/a “Double O,” 29, of Paterson, pled guilty to RICO conspiracy on March 3, 2026; Born Allah, a/k/a “Freedom,” 25, of Paterson (“B. Allah”), pled guilty to RICO conspiracy on November 5, 2025; Elijah Rubio, a/k/a “Lottery,” 22, of Paterson, pled guilty to RICO conspiracy on November 4, 2025; and Kyzeik Robinson, a/k/a “Doo Doo,” a/k/a “King Sparks,” 20, of Paterson, pled guilty to RICO conspiracy and conspiracy to distribute controlled substances on September 9, 2025. These charges and pleas are the result of a long-running investigation coordinated between the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the New Jersey State Police, the United States Postal Inspection Service, and the Passaic County Sheriff’s Office, among other law enforcement agencies. According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court: J. Allah, Thomas, Davis, Reyes, Robinson, Pitts, B. Allah, Rubio, Short, Byrd, and Franklin are all members and associates of the neighborhood-based street gang known as “100k,” which operates in the area of North Main Street and Jefferson Street in Paterson, New Jersey (the “100k Enterprise”).  Since in or around January 2021, these members and associates of the 100k Enterprise have engaged in numerous criminal acts in furtherance of their gang activity, including murder, shootings, robberies, drug trafficking, and bank and wire fraud. Since the gang’s founding in 2016, members and associates of the 100k Enterprise have engaged in acts of violence against members of rival gangs, such as their primary rival, “the Blockboyz,” which operates out of the Presidential Tower Housing Complex in Paterson, among other rival gangs, such as “4k,” which operates in the area of Rosa Parks Boulevard near Lyon Street, Keen Street, and Mercer Street, also in Paterson. Specifically, on or about October 1, 2023, in retaliation for the death of a high-ranking member of the 100k Enterprise, J. Allah, Thomas, Davis, and other members and associates of the 100k Enterprise shot and killed Victim-2, in territory controlled by the Blockboyz. On or about May 27, 2024, Pitts and other members and associates of the 100k Enterprise shot and injured Victim-3, a member of the rival gang “4k.” On or about October 3, 2024, Short exchanged fire with Victim-4 in territory controlled by the 100k Enterprise. Weeks later, on or about November 17, 2024, Short shot and injured Victim-5, a member of the Blockboyz, in territory controlled by the Blockboyz, and Byrd acted as the driver in that November shooting. The defendants raised money for themselves and the 100k Enterprise by engaging in robberies, drug trafficking, bank fraud, and other financial schemes. Two such robberies included: the armed robbery of a commercial marijuana store on or about January 13, 2022 by Reyes, B. Allah, Short, Rubio, and others; and the attempted armed robbery of Victim-1, a United States Postal Service employee, on or about July 28, 2023 by Reyes, who tried to obtain an arrow key from the victim. This arrow key would have allowed members of the 100k Enterprise to gain access to United States Postal Service mailboxes within a certain geographic area or postal route, which could be used to steal checks and credit cards from the mail in furtherance of the types of bank fraud scheme engaged in by 100k Enterprise members such as Thomas and Franklin. The gang’s drug trafficking activities were extensive, with investigators conducting 16 controlled buys with Reyes, Robinson, Davis, and Pitts by utilizing undercover officers and observing countless more drug deals committed by the defendants within and around the territory of Paterson controlled by the 100k Enterprise through physical surveillance and review of cell phone records and social media accounts controlled by the defendants. The charge of RICO conspiracy in Count One of the Superseding Indictment carries a maximum statutory penalty of life in prison as to J. Allah, Thomas, and Davis, and a maximum statutory penalty of 20 years in prison as to Reyes, Robinson, Pitts, B. Allah, Rubio, Short, Byrd, and Franklin. The additional count of conspiracy to distribute controlled substances in the Superseding Indictment to which Pitts and Robinson pled guilty carries a mandatory minimum term of 5 years in prison and a maximum penalty of 40 years in prison and a fine of at least $5 million. The count of assaulting or impeding certain United States officers or employees in the Superseding Indictment to which Reyes pled guilty carries a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment. The count of brandishing a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence in the Superseding Indictment to which Reyes pled guilty carries a mandatory minimum term of 7 years and a maximum term of life imprisonment. U.S. Attorney Frazer credited law enforcement members with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Newark Field Division, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Beau Kolodka; the New Jersey State Police, Gangs and Organized Crime North Unit, under the direction of Superintendent Jeanne Hengemuhle; the United States Postal Inspection Service, under the direction of Inspector in Charge Christopher Nielsen; the Passaic County Sheriff’s Office, under the direction of Sheriff Thomas Adamo; the Paterson Police Department, under the direction of Officer In Charge Patrick Murray; the Bergen County Sheriff’s Office under the direction of Sheriff Anthony Cureton; the Passaic County Prosecutor’s Office under the direction of Prosecutor Camelia M. Valdes; and the Bergen County Prosecutor’s Office under the direction of Prosecutor Mark Musella with the investigation. The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jake A. Nasar of the Healthcare Fraud and Opioid Enforcement Unit, and Eli Jacobs of the Organized Crime and Gangs Unit in Newark. ### Defense counsel: Alyssa A. Cimino & Jean D. Barrett, Esqs. for Jasun Allah John A. Azzarello & Perry Primavera, Esqs. for Michael Davis Joel Silverman & Troy A. Archie, Esqs. for Christopher Thomas Georgina Giordano Pallitoo, Esq. for Jazmier Reyes Joseph Z. Amsel, Esq. for Kyziek Robinson Rahul Agarwal, Esq. for Jacim Pitts Jason F. Orlando, Esq. for Born Allah Jason J. LeBoeuf, Esq. for Elijah Rubio Maximillian Novel, Esq. for Trasean Short Christopher D. Adams, Esq. for Elijah Byrd Andrew C. title: Grand Jury Indictments Returned Against Three Men with Ties to Halloween Shooting
body: Press Release Grand Jury Indictments Returned Against Three Men with Ties to Halloween Shooting Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Missouri JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. – A federal grand jury in Jefferson City, Mo., has returned indictments against three individuals with ties to an Oct. 31, 2026 shooting in Columbia, Mo. An indictment was returned alleging that Iseah Christopher Jackson, 23, possessed a firearm and ammunition on Oct. 31, 2026. Jackson had previously been charged by complaint, and the affidavit supporting the complaint alleged that Jackson had been identified by law enforcement as having been present during a shooting in the area of Ninth Street and Walnut Street in Columbia on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. Later that day, a traffic stop was conducted on his vehicle and a loaded Springfield HS Produkt Hellcat 9mm semi-automatic handgun was found in his glove compartment, and a single round of 9mm ammunition was in his pocket. Jackson was previously convicted of two counts of involuntary manslaughter and is not permitted to possess firearms or ammunition. Jackson has been detained by the court pending disposition of his criminal case. An indictment was also returned against Treyvale Damarcus Cain-Raybon, 21, alleging that he possessed two cartridge cases despite a prior felony conviction. Cain-Raybon was previously charged by complaint, and the supporting affidavit noted that he was identified on surveillance video in an alleyway at the time of the shooting on Oct. 31, 2026, pointing a firearm at another subject, then retreating to an area behind a vehicle and firing two times. Investigators later recovered Winchester 9mm shell casings in the area from which Cain-Raybon was firing. Cain-Raybon has a prior felony conviction for unlawful use of a weapon and has been detained by the court pending trial. Finally, the grand jury returned a two-count indictment against Detravion Latrell Coats, 21. One count of the indictment alleges that Coats possessed ammunition on Dec. 31, 2026. In a previously filed complaint affidavit, law enforcement alleged that Coats was identified on video as having been in the area of Ninth Street and Walnut Street in Columbia at the time of a shooting on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026, and was seen on the video firing over a vehicle at a group of individuals and discharging his weapon approximately ten times. Two Barnaul 9mm shell casings were later recovered from the area in which Coats was seen shooting. In a second count of the indictment returned by the grand jury yesterday, Coats was also charged with possessing a firearm and ammunition on Nov. 5, 2026. Coats has prior felony convictions for involuntary manslaughter, second degree assault, and resisting arrest, and due to these convictions, he is not permitted to possess firearms or ammunition. Coats has been detained by the court pending the disposition of his criminal charges. The charges contained in these indictments are accusations, and not evidence of guilt. Evidence supporting the charges must eventually be presented to a federal trial jury, whose duty it is to determine guilt or innocence. These cases are being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lauren E. Kummerer. It was investigated by the Columbia Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. Updated November 25, 2026 Topic Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Missouri, Western

title: Richmond, Vermont Man Charged with Being a Felon in Possession of a Firearm
body: Press Release Richmond, Vermont Man Charged with Being a Felon in Possession of a Firearm Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Vermont USAVT.Press@usdoj.gov BURLINGTON – The United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Vermont stated that Shawn M. Burnett, 34, of Richmond, Vermont, was charged yesterday by criminal complaint with unlawfully possessing a firearm as a convicted felon. Burnett’s initial appearance in federal court is currently scheduled for December 18, 2026, at 11 a.m. before United States Magistrate Judge Kevin J. Doyle in Burlington. According to court records, Burnett was a person of interest in various incidents involving stolen vehicles in Chittenden and Lamoille Counties, Vermont. Officers encountered Burnett on November 20, 2026, as he was driving a pickup truck that was allegedly stolen. Officers pursued Burnett and he then crashed into another vehicle in Barre City, Vermont. Burnett was found to be in possession of a Taurus .38 special revolver, which had been reported stolen from a different vehicle. Burnett is prohibited from possessing firearms due to prior felony convictions sustained in January 2026 in Chittenden County Superior Court. The United States Attorney’s Office emphasizes that the complaint contains allegations only and that Burnett is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty. Burnett faces up to 15 years of imprisonment if convicted. The actual sentence, however, would be determined by the District Court with guidance from the advisory United States Sentencing Guidelines and the statutory sentencing factors. First Assistant United States Attorney Jonathan A. Ophardt commended the investigatory efforts of the Barre City Police Department, the Vermont State Police, the Vermont Department of Fish and Wildlife, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. The prosecutor is Assistant United States Attorney Robert Shoemaker. Burnett’s current representation is unknown. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. title: The Government Successfully Forfeited Over $670,000 in Cryptocurrency  Linked to an Online Investment Scam
body: Press Release The Government Successfully Forfeited Over $670,000 in Cryptocurrency  Linked to an Online Investment Scam Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.gov Chief U.S. District Judge Brenda K. Sannes issued an order November 16, 2026, forfeiting $674,469.58 worth of cryptocurrency seized by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to the government in connection with an investigation of an online cryptocurrency scam affecting multiple victims. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III and Craig L. Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Albany Field Office for the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), made the announcement. According to the underlying complaint, in May of 2024, a victim in Onondaga County was contacted about participation in an online platform purporting to provide guidance on cryptocurrency trading techniques. The victim was tricked into transferring cryptocurrency into what they believed was a secure account on a cryptocurrency exchange linked to the platform. Soon thereafter, when the victim attempted to withdraw the cryptocurrency he transferred, he was unable to do so because the funds had been stolen. Further investigation by the FBI revealed several additional victims of the same fraudulent scheme, a type of scam known as “pig butchering.” Additional investigation by the FBI, including sophisticated cryptocurrency tracing, identified a cryptocurrency wallet linked to the scam that contained $674,469.58 worth of cryptocurrency, which was quickly seized by the FBI with the assistance of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of New York. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sarcone stated, “There is no doubt that the Court’s order comes as a great relief to the victims of this fraud scheme. I commend the FBI on their incredible work locating these funds and working with my office to seize and secure them, which will provide the victims with the opportunity to seek recovery of their stolen funds. My office remains committed to rooting out financial fraud in all forms and returning as much money as possible to victims.” “These types of fraud schemes remain a pervasive threat to hard-working Americans,” said Craig Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albany Field Office. “The FBI is committed to using every resource we have to investigate these fraudsters, bring them to justice, and – when possible – return the stolen funds to the victims. We encourage anyone who falls victim to these detrimental scams to immediately report the incident to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) so we can leverage our specialty teams and mitigate the losses.” Generally, in cases involving cryptocurrency, the U.S. Attorney’s Office first seeks to forfeit stolen funds and then works with the Department of Justice’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section to, in many cases, return forfeited funds to crime victims. The FBI investigated the case and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey D. Brown and Adrian LaRochelle represented the United States. Anyone who believes they are a victim of a cybercrime – including cryptocurrency scams, romance scams, and investment scams – should contact the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center at https://www.ic3.gov . Updated November 25, 2026 Topics Asset Forfeiture Cybercrime Fraud Component USAO - New York, Northern

title: Regulators implement growth-friendly securitisation reforms
body:
Regulators implement growth-friendly securitisation reforms | Bank of England – the UK's central bank Our use of cookies We use necessary cookies to make our site work. We’d also like to use some non-essential cookies (including third-party cookies) to help us improve the site. By clicking ‘Accept recommended settings’ on this banner, you accept our use of analytics cookies.   For more information on how these cookies work please see our Cookie policy . Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content Regulators implement growth-friendly securitisation reforms The Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority have today published revised rules designed to support securitisation’s contribution to economic growth. Published on  
        25 November 2026 News release The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) have today published revised rules designed to support securitisation’s contribution to economic growth. Securitisation allows a firm to divide loans into 'tranches' which have different risk profiles. Investors may buy some or all tranches, providing the firm with funding for further lending, while the interest from the loans pays the investors, who also absorb some of the losses when borrowers do not repay their loans. Securitisation can help firms manage their funding and risk, supporting further lending to businesses and households. Today’s changes are designed to make the regulators’ requirements more proportionate and less prescriptive, helping reduce unnecessary costs for firms, while maintaining financial stability. They include: Simplifying due diligence and transparency requirements, holding investors and issuers to the same standards of understanding and disclosing risks without being overly prescriptive; Introducing more flexible risk retention options, while ensuring firms keep at least 5% of a securitisation's value at risk; Allowing some simple and prudent re-securitisations to support firms' funding and liquidity needs, while continuing the ban on the wider practice. The reforms are also estimated to reduce industry costs by around £168 million over the next decade while maintaining important safeguards and high standards. Phil Evans, Director of Prudential Policy at the Prudential Regulation Authority, said: 'Securitisation is an important part of a modern financial system. It is obvious that we must never go back to the dangerous practices in place before the great financial crisis, but we shouldn’t go too far the other way either and stifle lending. Today’s final rules strike that balance and should encourage firms to lend more to households and businesses.' Jon Relleen, Director of Infrastructure and Exchanges at the Financial Conduct Authority, said: 'Strong capital markets are vital to support economic growth. By simplifying the UK's securitisation regime, we’re reducing unnecessary costs, giving firms and investors greater flexibility, and better reflecting market practice. The changes support more effective markets but crucially also maintain high standards to mitigate potential risks.' Notes to editors Read the full policy statement . The FCA has published near-final rules as part of its reforms to the UK securitisation framework. This policy statement follows a number of recent PRA and FCA measures aimed at supporting growth, competitiveness and innovation in UK financial services while maintaining financial stability, including, exploring ideas to support the growth of credit unions; simplifying the Senior Managers & Certification regime; and automatically increasing over 100 PRA regulatory thresholds to provide certainty for firms. The FCA has published near-final rules as part of its reforms to the UK securitisation framework. The rules are near-final because the related statutory instrument has been laid by HM Treasury but has not yet been made. The FCA intends to make the final rules shortly after the statutory instrument has been made and does not expect any significant changes to them. The PRA has published final rules at the same time. For further details of estimated costs saving, please refer to the cost benefit analyses set out in FCA Consultation Paper CP26/6 . title: Card payments edge past cash in shops; euro area consumers want both
body:
Card payments edge past cash in shops; euro area consumers want both Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date PRESS RELEASE Card payments edge past cash in shops; euro area consumers want both 25 November 2026 Physical cards account for 45% of payments in shops, compared with 44% for cash Cash remains especially important for small value payments and payments between individuals Ability to pay digitally and with cash are both important to consumers The European Central Bank (ECB) today published its latest study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area (SPACE). The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. For the first time since comparable data were collected in 2016, [ 1 ] cards were used more often than cash at physical locations, such as shops. In 2026 cards accounted for 45% of transactions, compared with 44% for cash. Mobile payments increased to 9%, from 6% in 2024. While payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences remain stable. When paying in a shop, 54% preferred cards or other cashless methods, 22% preferred cash and 23% had no clear preference. A large majority of respondents attach importance to retaining a choice of payment methods. For 82% of euro area consumers, it is important to have the option to pay digitally, while 62% value the option of paying with cash. Only 3% reported never using cash. “Digital means of payment are becoming more important in day-to-day transactions, but choice is what really matters for Europeans,” said Piero Cipollone, member of the ECB’s Executive Board. “The ECB will continue to ensure citizens have the freedom to choose how to pay, by safeguarding cash while preparing for the possible issuance of its digital equivalent, the digital euro.” Most consumers continue to find it easy to access cash, although the share declined to 85%, from 87% in 2024. Among those who had tried to withdraw cash from an ATM during the previous year, 19% experienced difficulties. In all euro area countries, at least 12% of consumers experienced non-acceptance of mobile or card payments at least once in the month preceding the survey. The survey covered 51,551 respondents across the euro area. Data were collected in two rounds: the first between 29 September and 27 November 2025, and the second between 16 March and 15 May 2026. For media queries, please contact Alessandro Speciale , tel.: +49 172 1670791. Previous editions of the SPACE study were published in 2019, 2022 and 2024. In 2016 the ECB published a study on the use of cash by households in the euro area (SUCH). title: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability.
body: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability. Oran Kelly Research Scientist, Google DeepMind Nov 24, 2026 Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings. Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE. Explore the live leaderboard , or read our technical report . To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week Kaggle competition through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong. Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue)

title: November 23, 2026 - FDA Approves First New Hormone Therapy for Early-Stage Breast Cancer in More Than 20 Years
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First New Hormone Therapy for Early-Stage Breast Cancer in More Than 20 Years For Immediate Release: November 23, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Wilserdly (giredestrant), used alone after surgery in adults with estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer — the most common subtype of the disease. A once-daily oral tablet, Wilserdly is the first new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer in more than 20 years. Wilserdly belongs to a class of medicines called oral estrogen receptor antagonists. In estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer, estrogen binds to receptors (proteins) on cancer cells and signals them to grow. Estrogen receptor antagonists like Wilserdly block this process and break down the receptors, cutting off a key driver of tumor growth. “Like many Americans, I have seen breast cancer affect my own family. That experience makes the work we do at FDA deeply personal,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Even as we recognize how far treatment has come for early-stage breast cancer, the Trump administration knows that patients and their families are counting on us to keep building on that progress, and that’s what we’ve done with today’s approval.” The approval covers adults with estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative, stage I, II, or III disease with an intermediate to high risk of recurrence following surgery. Breast cancer is the second most common cancer among women in the United States. An estimated 321,910 new cases are expected in women and 2,670 in men in 2026, approximately 70% of which are estrogen receptor–positive and HER2-negative. “For patients with early-stage hormone-driven breast cancer, the goal after surgery is to keep the cancer from coming back,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “Our review focused on whether Wilserdly could reduce that risk more effectively than the hormone therapies patients already receive. The evidence showed that it could, supporting today’s approval of a new option for patients at intermediate to high risk of recurrence.” In the randomized, multicenter lidERA Breast Cancer trial ( NCT04961996 ), 4,170 adults with this subtype at intermediate to high risk of recurrence were assigned to receive Wilserdly or standard of care hormone therapy — tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole, letrozole, or exemestane) for up to 5 years. Wilserdly reduced the risk of invasive breast cancer recurrence or death by 30% compared with standard hormone therapy (140 versus 196 patients experienced an event during follow-up). This made lidERA the first phase III trial to demonstrate a benefit with an oral estrogen receptor antagonist in early-stage breast cancer. At 3 years, 92.4% of patients taking Wilserdly were alive and free of invasive breast cancer, compared with 89.6% of those taking standard hormone therapy. This translates to about 28 more patients out of every 1,000 alive and free of invasive breast cancer at 3 years. Patients receiving Wilserdly also had a lower risk of cancer returning in another part of the body. Patients are being followed to determine whether Wilserdly helps them live longer. The applicant has agreed to submit these results to the FDA as a postmarketing commitment . The FDA previously approved Wilserdly on November 16, 2026, in combination with everolimus for certain adults with estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated advanced or metastatic breast cancer whose disease recurred or progressed during or after prior endocrine therapy. That approval was based on the evERA Breast Cancer trial ( NCT05306340 ). The most common side effects (≥10%) of Wilserdly are muscle and joint pain, hot flashes, tiredness, headache, nausea, slower-than-normal heart rate, dizziness, numbness or tingling in the hands and feet. Common blood test changes include increased liver enzymes, lower blood counts, high blood fat levels, and changes in mineral levels and kidney test results. Wilserdly may harm a developing baby if taken during pregnancy. Women who have not completed menopause should also receive an additional hormone-suppressing medicine with Wilserdly. Men may also receive this medicine, as determined by their healthcare provider. The FDA’s evaluation of the application was supported by an Assessment Aid voluntarily submitted by the applicant. The FDA granted Priority Review to the application. The approval was granted to Genentech, Inc, a member of the Roche Group. Media: FDA Request for Comment 202-690-6343 Consumer: 888-INFO-FDA The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products. ###

title: Treasury Identifies Nearly $15 Billion in Potential Iranian Shadow Banking
body: November 23, 2026 WASHINGTON —In a new Financial Trend Analysis , the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) identified approximately $14.7 billion of financial activity from January 2025 to August 2026 potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking. As part of their compliance requirements, U.S. financial institutions flag suspicious activity to FinCEN, making it available to law enforcement and national security agencies. “Financial institutions are often the first line of defense in denying Iranian regime-linked funds access to the U.S. economy,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent . “Treasury will continue to sever the financial lifelines on which the regime relies to fund its military, weapons programs, and terror proxies.” The trends and methods associated with potential Iranian shadow banking remained relatively consistent through 2026. Potential Iranian shadow banking networks continue to be connected across continents, most prominently in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Hong Kong, and Singapore, and by the oil, shipping, investment, technology procurement, and other industries. Key Findings The most common routes for funds flagged by financial institutions were: from mainland China-based banks to UAE-based banks: approximately $2.6 billion; Singapore-based banks to UAE-based banks: approximately $981 million; and United Kingdom-based banks to UAE-based banks: approximately $922 million. The potential exploitation of companies registered in the Marshall Islands and British Virgin Islands, usually at addresses linked to corporate registries, emerged as an area of concern. Potential Iran-linked companies were involved in a diverse array of businesses, including shipping, trading, and oil. Reporting Suspicious Iran-Related Activity To support financial institutions in their Bank Secrecy Act reporting, FinCEN has previously issued several publications that highlight red flags on Iran-linked actors: FinCEN Advisory on the Iranian Regime’s Illicit Oil Smuggling Activities, Shadow Banking Networks, and Weapons Procurement Efforts (June 2025) FinCEN Alert on the Use of Front Companies, Financial Facilitators, and Digital Asset Infrastructure by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to Evade Sanctions and Launder Proceeds (May 2026) FinCEN Alert to Counter Iranian Procurement Efforts for its Commercial Aviation Industry (September 2026) FinCEN Alert to Counter Iranian Abuse of Religious Charity Networks (October 2026) Through its whistleblower incentive program , FinCEN welcomes tips on Iran-related illicit finance . Individuals located in the United States or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations may be eligible for an award if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000. As highlighted in FinCEN’s recent Bulletin ( available in several languages ), this includes information about violations of the Bank Secrecy Act or Office of Foreign Assets Control-administered sanctions programs that may involve the use of Iranian proxies and facilitators operating outside of Iran. ###

title: Operation Economic Outcast Disrupts Iran’s Global Shadow Banking Networks
body: November 23, 2026 WASHINGTON —Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury sanctioned over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel in a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran’s global shadow banking networks. As Iran’s economy remains battered by punishing economic sanctions and its oil revenues continue to decline, the regime’s shadow banking facilitators have increasingly failed to repatriate dwindling export earnings while simultaneously enriching themselves by stealing state resources that rightfully belong to the Iranian people. “Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent . “Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake.” Today’s action targets the financial infrastructure that underpins much of Iran’s remaining foreign trade, disrupting the exchange houses, front companies, and facilitators that move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions. This action is being taken pursuant to the following Executive Orders (E.O.): E.O. 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, including Iran’s financial sector; E.O. 13224, as amended, a counter-terrorism designation authority; and E.O. 13871, which targets persons operating in various sectors of Iran’s metals industry. OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026, dubbed Economic D-Day, Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime. Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror. Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. Operation Economic Outcast significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran.  Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system. It also expanded secondary sanctions exposure for those who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here . EXCHANGE HOUSES AND RAHBAR COMPANIES Iran’s shadow banking system is overseen by the Central Bank of Iran and relies on dozens of Iran-based exchange houses and “rahbar companies,” bank affiliates that manage sanctions evasion networks for their Iran-based clients. Exchange houses and rahbar companies work hand-in-hand to facilitate the financial underpinnings of Iran’s international trade through thousands of front companies in multiple jurisdictions, most prominently, but not exclusively, in Dubai and Hong Kong. Billions of dollars move through the international financial system in this fashion, sustaining the last remnants of Iran’s foreign trade. Iran-based Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company (Nesim Baharan) operates as the rahbar company for Bank Sarmayeh and works closely with Iranian exchange houses and their front companies to facilitate transactions on behalf of Bank Sarmayeh’s Iranian clients, which include major Iranian petrochemical companies. Sayyed Mohammad Jalali , Valiollah Hemmati , and Ali Kalhor act as senior officials of Nesim Baharan. Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Sayyed Mohammad Jalali, Valiollah Hemmati, and Ali Kalhor are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company. Iran-based Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company (Fashki Exchange) and Mellat Exchange Company are exchange houses operating within Iran’s shadow banking system. Mina Fashki and Farzad Fashki own and operate Fashki Exchange, while Mahmoud Akhlaghi , Parviz Fazlju , and Mohammad Hossein Abbasi are officials of Mellat Exchange Company. Note : This graphic updates an April 2026 version to include Bank Sarmayeh and its rahbar. Fashki Exchange and Mellat Exchange Company are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Mina Fashki and Farzad Fashki are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Fashki Exchange. Mahmoud Akhlaghi, Parviz Fazlju, and Mohammad Hossein Abbasi are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Mellat Exchange Company. Dubai-based Grand Target Heavy Equipment and Machinery Spare Parts Trading L.L.C , Recaz Star General Trading LLC , Meethale Raw Materials Trading Company LLC , Hemraj Trading L.L.C , Ewan Al Madeena General Trading LLC , OGA Global General Trading L.L.C , Dexterous Global DMCC , Khore Al Hilal Goods Wholesalers Trading LLC , Türkiye-based Bogazici Gumrukleme Ithalat Ihracat Turizm Petrol Urunleri Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi , and Hong Kong-based Grandez Trading Limited are exchange house front companies used by Iran’s rahbar network to facilitate thousands of cross-border payments, worth billions of dollars, on behalf of Iranian clients. These front companies have enabled Iran to carry out thousands of financial transactions through the rahbar network. Khore Al Hilal Goods Wholesalers Trading LLC has been used extensively by U.S.-sanctioned Iranian exchange houses Opal Exchange, also known as Pedram Pirouzan Exchange , and Omid Sepah Exchange to move millions of dollars for Iranian Bank Sepah. Grandez Trading Limited is a front company used by the U.S.-sanctioned Iranian exchange house Mohsen Khandan and Partners Exchange . Recaz Star General Trading LLC has sent and received hundreds of payments totaling over $170 million from persons associated with Sadaf Exchange . OGA Global General Trading LLC has overseen millions of dollars’ worth of payments for the National Iranian Tanker Company , which operates Iran’s fleet of state-owned oil tankers. Grand Target Heavy Equipment and Machinery Spare Parts Trading L.L.C, Recaz Star General Trading LLC, Meethale Raw Materials Trading Company LLC, Hemraj Trading L.L.C, Ewan Al Madeena General Trading LLC, OGA Global General Trading L.L.C, Dexterous Global DMCC, Khore Al Hilal Goods Wholesalers Trading LLC, Bogazici Gumrukleme Ithalat Ihracat Turizm Petrol Urunleri Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi, and Grandez Trading Limited are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. SHADOW BANKING FRONT COMPANIES Iranian exchange houses and rahbar companies operate through a multi-jurisdictional web of layered front and shell companies that enable them to remit and receive payments overseas on behalf of their Iranian customers. Iranian companies that participate in the global economy, in some way or fashion, engage with the Iranian shadow banking system to facilitate imports and exports. For example, Dubai-based Robust Trading LLC has facilitated payments for the sanctioned Iran-based copper mining giant National Iranian Copper Industries Company . Similarly, HMS Trading FZE , the Dubai-based oil export and commercial front company of Iranian Shahr Bank, has used Dubai-based Integral Petro Energy Trading LLC to facilitate millions of dollars’ worth of liquefied petroleum gas sales by Iranian petrochemical exporter Kharg Petrochemical Company Limited. Robust Trading LLC is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13871 for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services in support of, the National Iranian Copper Industries Company. Integral Petro Energy Trading LLC is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, HMS Trading FZE. Other Dubai-based front companies include Royah Altahabia Trading L.L.C , Alam Al Sahra Building Materials Trading Co. L.L.C , Berkeley Trading LLC , and Nordic International Trading LLC , which have been counterparties to millions of dollars’ worth of transactions involving Iranian financial broker front companies operating within Iran’s rahbar system. Since at least 2022, Berkeley Trading L.L.C has facilitated millions of dollars’ worth of transactions for clients of Iran-based Amin Exchange. Royah Altahabia Trading L.L.C, Alam Al Sahra Building Materials Trading Co. L.L.C, Berkeley Trading LLC, and Nordic International Trading LLC are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Dubai-based Gespl International General Trading LLC has been used by the National Iranian Oil Company as part of its oil and petrochemicals sales mechanism and is actively involved in money laundering via Iran’s shadow banking mechanism. Gespl International General Trading LLC is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petrochemical sector of the Iranian economy. Iran’s military organs also utilize the shadow banking system. Iranian Armed Forces General Staff-associated Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company (SEJ) and sanctioned shipping company Dragon Road Ltd utilized Dubai-based H N B Trading Co LLC to complete payment for the charter of the SERENE I (IMO 9197832); H N B Trading Co LLC received hundreds of thousands of dollars from a SEJ front company as part of this scheme. H N B Trading Co LLC is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company. IRAN CENTER FOR EXCHANGE Additionally, as part of today’s action, OFAC is taking action against the Iran-based Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold (Iran Center for Exchange), which plays an essential intermediary role within Iran’s system of international trade. The Iran Center for Exchange provides the financial plumbing to match exporters, who earn foreign currency from sales abroad, to importers, who need foreign currency to purchase goods, for tens of billions of dollars’ worth of trade every year. While Iran’s shadow banking system moves the funds generated by Iran’s international trade, the Iran Center for Exchange plays matchmaker and guides these funds to their ultimate destination inside Iran. The Central Bank of Iran also utilizes bonds issued by the Iran Center for Exchange to help facilitate international trade using Russian roubles and Chinese yuan without reliance on the U.S. dollar. The Iran Center for Exchange is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s OFAC action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.   OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions, unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades or conspires to violate U.S. sanctions.  Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000. Financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities with designated or otherwise blocked persons, including the persons designated today.  This includes, in addition to blocking prohibitions, that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List, when consistent with relevant statutes and other authorities.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is to bring about a positive change in behavior.  What constitutes a sufficient change in circumstance will vary based on context, including the status of the broader geopolitical circumstances affecting the national security and foreign policy interests implicated by the declared national emergency.  In the case of sanctions related to Iran, OFAC is employing all available statutory, regulatory, and policy tools to resolve the persistent national emergencies posed by Iran, which has not changed its behavior to align with U.S. national security and foreign policy objectives.  OFAC sanctions determinations, including removal determinations, are made consistent with Administration foreign policy and national security policies and priorities.  For more information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on How to Request Removal from an OFAC List. title: November 23, 2026 - FDA Approves First Treatment for Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy Type 2I/R9
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First Treatment for Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy Type 2I/R9 For Immediate Release: November 23, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Welgemda (ribitol), the first medicine for treating limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9 (LGMD2I/R9), a rare inherited muscle disease, for adults and pediatric patients weighing at least 30 kg. Welgemda is the first therapy approved for any form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. “Today’s approval is a historic milestone for patients and families living with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, delivering the first-ever FDA-approved treatment for this disease, backed by clinical evidence,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Under the Trump Administration’s commitment to accelerating innovation and removing unnecessary barriers for rare disease therapies, while maintaining high standards for safety, the FDA is proud to deliver real hope and meaningful progress for patients who have waited far too long for options.” LGMD2I/R9 is caused by mutations in the FKRP gene, which disrupt a key biological process in muscle cells. In healthy individuals, the FKRP enzyme helps attach sugar molecules to a protein called alpha-dystroglycan, which acts as an anchor, helping muscle cells connect to surrounding tissue. When this process is disrupted, muscle cells become fragile and break down over time, leading to progressive weakness, difficulty walking, and in many patients, impaired breathing. Symptoms typically appear in childhood or early adulthood and worsen over time. “Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is a progressive muscle disease that gradually takes away a patient’s ability to walk, breathe, and live independently, often beginning in childhood,” said Laura Jawidzik, M.D., Director of the Division of Neurology 2 in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “The clinical data supporting Welgemda's approval show meaningful improvements in walking speed and lung function, and we are encouraged by what that can mean for patients' daily lives.” The precise mechanism of Welgemda in the treatment of LGMD2I/R9 is not fully known, but may involve increases in a natural sugar molecule (matriglycan) that anchors alpha-dystroglycan in muscle tissue. The medicine is taken as an oral solution twice daily, mixed with water. Welgemda was evaluated in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study ( NCT05775848 ) involving 112 patients with genetically confirmed LGMD2I/R9. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either Welgemda or placebo for up to 36 months. At a planned interim analysis after 12 months of treatment, patients receiving Welgemda showed significant improvements in two key measures compared to those receiving placebo. Specifically, patients showed improvements in walking speed, measured by the 100-meter timed test, and lung function, measured by forced vital capacity (an indicator of respiratory muscle health). Patients treated with Welgemda also showed significant increases in glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan, indicating the drug was reaching its intended target at the proposed dose. The most common adverse reactions were gastrointestinal effects (e.g., diarrhea, stomach pain) and joint pain. Welgemda received Orphan Drug , Fast Track , and rare pediatric disease designations for the treatment of LGMD2I/R9. Welgemda is manufactured by ML Bio Solutions Inc. and distributed by BridgeBio Pharma, Inc. Media: FDA Request for Comment 202-690-6343 Consumer: 888-INFO-FDA ### Boilerplate The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

title: Operation Economic Outcast Targets Corrupt Regime Insiders Exploiting Iran’s Oil Sector for Personal Gain
body: November 20, 2026 WASHINGTON —Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury is targeting key “oil trustees” the Iranian regime relies on to facilitate the sale of oil abroad. With no oil on the water outside of the U.S. military blockade and no oil loaded onto vessels since the start of Operation Economic Outcast, the regime is attempting to recoup billions of dollars from its oil trustees.  In many cases, these corrupt trustees have kept the oil revenue for personal gain. “Iran’s tyrannical regime never fails to put its own interests before those of its own citizens, even as ordinary Iranians face shortages of bread and fuel,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “The regime has exhausted its seaborne oil supply, and it may never see the revenue from the oil it has already sold. The ship is sinking.” The designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy, and E.O. 13224, as amended, a counterterrorism authority. OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026, dubbed Economic D-Day , Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime.  Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror.  Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. Operation Economic Outcast has also expanded sanctions exposure for non-U.S. persons who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here . UNTRUSTWORTHY TRUSTEES Mohammad Javad Bavand (Bavand) and Majid Taj (Taj), the brother of the Iranian Football Federation’s president, operate as part of a network of regime insiders tasked with obtaining desperately needed cash by selling from Iran’s dwindling oil reserves.  Bavand, a former IRGC intelligence officer, has spearheaded this effort, entrusting a group of personal contacts, including Taj, to recoup Iran’s oil funds located in third countries.  The Iranian regime continues to entrust Bavand and Taj’s network with facilitating Iran’s oil sales, despite members owing billions of dollars to the regime from previous sales.  Bavand has worked with a variety of illicit oil trading actors, including the IRGC and Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company (SEJ), a U.S.-designated front company tasked with selling oil for the Iranian Armed Forces General Staff. Mohammad Javad Bavand and Majid Taj are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy. REGIME FACILITATORS Mohammadhossein Servati (Servati), the son of IRGC Brigadier General Mohsen Servati, has held executive positions at companies operated by SEJ, including SEJ front company Xin Rui Jin Trad Co., Limited , and Sepehr Energy Hamta Pars , a subsidiary of SEJ.  Xin Rui Jin Trad Co., Limited brokered and received shipments of Iranian oil on behalf of SEJ for delivery to Chinese teapot refineries. Mohammadhossein Servati is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company. Mojtaba Arabnejad (Mojtaba) is the son of the designated Iranian businessman and CEO of Iran’s Mahan Air , Hamid Arabnejad .  Using his familial ties and special connections with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF), Mojtaba has been involved in purchasing aircraft parts for Mahan Air and procuring weapons for the Iranian military under the auspices of agricultural companies.  Like others designated today, Mojtaba has overseen oil sales for the Iranian regime, the proceeds from which have supported Mahan Air. Mojtaba Arabnejad is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Mahan Air. title: Treasury Sanctions Major Drug Trafficking Organizations Supporting Terrorist Cartels
body: November 19, 2026 Coordinated Action with International Partners Targets a Cartel-Linked Outlaw Motorcycle Gang and Canadian-Based Mafia Leaders and Facilitators WASHINGTON —Today, the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned two international drug trafficking organizations: the Australia-headquartered Comanchero Outlaw Motorcycle Gang ( Comancheros ) and the Italy-based ‘Ndrangheta , a mafia-type criminal syndicate.  By providing essential logistical and operational support, the Comancheros and ‘Ndrangheta help terrorist cartels expand their international reach and sustain global narcotrafficking networks. “Cartels do not operate in isolation. They rely on other criminal organizations like the Comancheros and ‘Ndrangheta to move drugs, launder illicit proceeds, and ultimately poison Americans with narcotics,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “Treasury will continue to expose and disrupt narcoterrorism networks to Keep America Safe.” The Comancheros and the ‘Ndrangheta operate sophisticated transnational criminal networks that facilitate large-scale drug trafficking and money laundering. The ‘Ndrangheta controls a significant share of the European cocaine trade, while the Comancheros have helped open access to some of the world's most lucrative illicit drug markets. In keeping with President Trump’s pledge to eliminate cartels, OFAC has prioritized targeting these and other criminal groups that threaten the welfare of Americans. Treasury has coordinated closely with the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF), taking nearly 40 actions against over 500 individuals and entities since the beginning of 2025.  OFAC uses a network-based approach to simultaneously disrupt as many different facets of the cartels as possible, from their leadership and key organizational nodes to facilitators and enablers, such as corrupt officials, complicit family members, and ostensibly legitimate front persons. Today’s action reflects a unified, whole-of-government effort to ensure operational coordination and maximize impact against transnational criminal networks.  OFAC conducted its investigation in parallel with the HSTF, with support from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Drug Enforcement Administration, and Homeland Security Investigations.  OFAC continues to work closely with the HSTF to disrupt the flow of illicit drugs and dismantle the networks, facilitators, and financial infrastructure that enable their production and distribution. Additionally, OFAC worked closely with valued international partners, including the Australian Federal Police, New Zealand Police, Italy’s Guardia di Finanza, and Canada’s Royal Canadian Mounted Police and York Regional Police, whose cooperation was instrumental in supporting today’s action. The action was taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 14059, which targets the proliferation of illicit drugs and their means of production. COMANCHERO OUTLAW MOTORCYCLE GANG Today, OFAC designated the Comancheros , also known as the Comanchero Motorcycle Club or simply Comanchero MC , an Australian drug trafficking organization with an international footprint in Asia, Europe, and North America.  Developing strategic partnerships with U.S. sanctioned cartels, including the Sinaloa Cartel, CJNG, Clan del Golfo, and Los Choneros, the Comancheros have facilitated multi-hundred-kilogram shipments of cocaine from South America to the United States, Australia, and Europe.  The Comancheros have also been involved in other criminal activity around the world, including assassinations, arms trafficking, and money laundering. Because Australia and New Zealand are some of the world’s most lucrative illicit drug markets, Mexican cartels are increasingly targeting these markets to capitalize on the significantly higher margins and growing demand.  Due to the geographic distance from the major cocaine producing regions in the Western Hemisphere, cartels can charge substantial premiums compared to drugs sold in the United States.  The Sinaloa Cartel has been known to send “sleeper cells” to Australia to facilitate local drug distribution and establish contacts with the Comancheros and other outlaw motorcycle gangs who assist with the logistics of drug trafficking. The Comancheros are being designated under E.O. 14059 for having engaged in, or having attempted to engage in, activities or transactions that have materially contributed to, or pose a significant risk of materially contributing to, the international proliferation of illicit drugs or their means of production. COMANCHERO COMMAND AND CONTROL Alexandre Varela Villar , better known as Alex Vare ( Vare ), is the Spain-based World Commander of the Comancheros. Allan John Norman Meehan , better known as Allan Meehan ( Meehan ), is the Australia-based World President of the Comancheros. Pasilika Naufahu ( Pasilika ) is the national president of the New Zealand chapter of the Comancheros.  Before being deported to New Zealand in 2016, Pasilika was the sergeant-at-arms of the Comancheros in Australia.  Pasilika was arrested and sentenced to 10 years in prison in February 2021 for various charges related to his position in the Comancheros.  In close coordination with his brother and senior Comancheros member, Vetekina Naufahu ( Vetekina ), Pasilika has facilitated multi-hundred-kilogram importations of drugs into New Zealand and has established connections to the Sinaloa Cartel. Marco Francis Coffen ( Coffen ) is an associate of the Comancheros and has been involved in supplying multiple Australian criminal organizations, including the Comancheros, with encrypted communication platforms to drug traffickers and shielding them from police phone taps. Vare and Meehan are being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for being or having been leaders or officials of the Comancheros. Pasilika and Vetekina are being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, the Comancheros. Coffen is being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having provided, or attempted to provide, financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services in support of, the Comancheros. OMERTÀ – THE ‘NDRANGHETA The ‘Ndrangheta , an international drug trafficking organization and mafia-type criminal syndicate, operates in over 80 countries and continues to grow.  The ‘Ndrangheta’s adherence to omertà , a code of silence, and its reliance on deeply rooted familial bloodlines have enabled the organization to maintain secrecy, foster loyalty, resist infiltration, and expand its criminal influence across generations and international borders.  While the ‘Ndrangheta was founded in Calabria, Italy, the organization has expanded across Europe, the Western Hemisphere, and Australia.  As one of the largest criminal organizations in the world, the ‘Ndrangheta’s primary business comes from drug trafficking, with some estimates stating that almost 80 percent of the European cocaine trade is controlled by the ‘Ndrangheta.  While primarily focused on the cocaine trade, Italian officials have stated that the ‘Ndrangheta have started expanding into the illicit fentanyl market. The ’Ndrangheta frequently partner with Mexican and South American drug trafficking organizations and FTOs, including the Sinaloa Cartel, CJNG, and Clan del Golfo.  In the past, the ‘Ndrangheta has also partnered with other Mexican drug trafficking organizations and FTOs, including Los Zetas (now known as Cartel del Noreste) and the Gulf Cartel. The ‘Ndrangheta was previously designated on May 30, 2008 , pursuant to the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act (Kingpin Act).  Today, the ‘Ndrangheta is being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having engaged in, or having attempted to engage in, activities or transactions that have materially contributed to, or pose a significant risk of materially contributing to, the international proliferation of illicit drugs or their means of production. ‘NDRANGHETISTI NORTH OF THE BORDER Locali (singular: locale ) are the primary territorial organizational unit of the ‘Ndrangheta, comprising members known as ‘ ndranghetisti , that oversee and coordinate criminal activities within a specific geographical region.  The ‘Ndrangheta locale that operates in the Greater Toronto Area in Canada has strengthened in recent years, becoming so powerful that they dictate events in Italy from across the ocean.  In Canada, the ‘Ndrangheta is involved in drug trafficking, money laundering, murder, and other crimes.  This faction of the ‘Ndrangheta uses the U.S. and Canadian financial systems to launder illicit proceeds. Today, OFAC designated Italian-born Angelo Figliomeni (also known as “Don Angelino”), the leader of the Toronto faction of the ‘Ndrangheta.  A member of the Figliomeni ‘ndrina (family), Angelo Figliomeni fled to Canada in the early 2000’s to escape a 20-year sentence for weapons charges in Italy.  Angelo’s power extends beyond Canada, stretching back to Italy.  He has engaged in money laundering and other criminal activities on behalf of the ‘Ndrangheta. Another member of the Figliomeni ‘ndrina is Italian-born Cosimo Figliomeni (sometimes known as “Cosimino”), who is a top leader of the ‘Ndrangheta faction in Toronto and has been the subject of criminal proceedings in Italy in connection to his role within the ‘Ndrangheta organization. OFAC also designated two members of the Commisso ‘ndrina who are long time Italian-born leaders of the ‘Ndrangheta in Toronto. Francesco Commisso , also known as “U Scelto,” has faced allegations in Italy of being part of a Toronto oversight body that was tasked, among other duties, with imposing disciplinary sanctions on members. Rocco Remo Commisso (also known as Remo Commisso ) is a Canada-based leader of the ‘Ndrangheta and leads narcotics trafficking networks within the United States, including in the state of New York.  Remo Commisso was convicted in Canada in 1981 for conspiracy to commit murder and again in 1984 for his involvement in a bombing that killed one person.  Remo Commisso is involved in narcotics trafficking in the United States for the ‘Ndrangheta, including in New York. Vincenzo DeMaria (also known as Jimmy DeMaria ) is one of Toronto’s top ‘Ndrangheta bosses and has been active in the Toronto organized crime scene for decades.  DeMaria shot and killed a man in 1981 over a $2,000 drug debt and was convicted of second-degree murder in 1982.  He has since been released from prison and holds significant power in the ‘Ndrangheta. Cosimo Figliomeni, Francesco Commisso, Remo Commisso, and Jimmy DeMaria make up the Camera di Controllo of Toronto, a collegial body of the ‘Ndrangheta that decides on important questions concerning the organization and settles disputes, even outside of Toronto.  The Toronto ‘Ndrangheta is tightly connected throughout the world and has close relationships with members back in Calabria. Luigi Vescio Sr. (also known as “The Undertaker” or “Lui Vescio”) is a Canadian-born ‘Ndrangheta senior member and associate of Angelo Figliomeni and Jimmy DeMaria. Angelo Figliomeni, Cosimo Figliomeni, Francesco Commisso, Remo Commisso, and Luigi Vescio Sr. were all charged in the Italian Court of Reggio Calabria for mafia-type association related to their leadership, membership, and promotion of the ‘Ndrangheta in 2019. Angelo Figliomeni, Cosimo Figliomeni, Francesco Commisso, Remo Commisso, Jimmy DeMaria, and Luigi Vescio Sr. are being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, ‘Ndrangheta. FAMILY-OWNED, MAFIA-CONNECTED – VESCIO FUNERAL HOMES OFAC is also designating the corporate network of Vescio Sr., including his network of funeral homes in Ontario.  These funeral homes include the Fratelli Vescio Funeral Homes Ltd. in Woodbridge, Ontario, Vescio Funeral Homes Ltd. in Toronto and Vescio Funeral Home (Maple) Inc. in Maple, Ontario.  Vescio Sr. also controls a Toronto-based luxury limousine rental business, Phantom Limousine Services Inc. Vescio Sr. serves as the president of each of these companies. OFAC is also designating Luigi Vescio Sr.’s wife, Rose Vescio , and his two children, Luigi Vescio Jr. and Laura Vescio , for their roles in owning and operating the Vescio Funeral Homes on behalf of Luigi Vescio Sr. Rose Vescio, Luigi Vescio Jr., and Laura Vescio are being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Luigi Vescio Sr. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  Unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  In addition, financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities involving designated or otherwise blocked persons.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List), but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior.  For information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on Filing a Petition for Removal from an OFAC List .
